name: Methodist movement (England)
notes: Methodism began as a renewal movement within the Church of England in the 18th century.
summary: An eighteenth-century renewal movement emphasizing conversion, disciplined Christian fellowship, and practical holiness.
formation_narrative: John and Charles Wesley worked within the Church of England while organizing societies and preaching beyond ordinary parish settings. Regular meetings, lay leadership, and hymns helped participants sustain a demanding devotional life. John Wesley’s 1738 assurance experience is a major milestone, not the only possible beginning of Methodism. Separate Methodist institutions developed gradually; the movement should not simply be treated as dissolved when new churches emerged.
core_beliefs: Grace and response: salvation begins with God’s grace, calls for faith, and leads into a transformed life.
Holiness: love of God and neighbor is the aim of Christian growth, not merely formal membership.
Connectional practice: preaching, sacraments, disciplined fellowship, and mission join personal faith to shared church life.

key_figures.name: John Wesley
key_figures.summary: An Anglican minister and organizer of Methodist societies who linked the message of grace to disciplined discipleship and growth in love.

key_figures.name: Charles Wesley
key_figures.summary: An Anglican minister and prolific hymn writer whose songs taught Methodist theology and helped sustain its devotional and congregational life.

key_dates.label: John Wesley’s Aldersgate experience becomes a defining spiritual milestone
American Methodist organization gains a separate institutional form

key_documents.title: Wesleyan sermons and doctrinal heritage
key_documents.significance: Foundational teaching about grace and holiness; the exact collection and constitutional status vary among Methodist churches.

key_documents.title: Articles of Religion
key_documents.significance: Wesley’s adaptation of Anglican articles supplied a doctrinal foundation for American Methodism; later bodies retained this heritage in different constitutional settings.

profile_scope: This is an introductory profile. It distinguishes shared teaching from historical development; sources do not imply that every member held an identical position. No formal corporate dissolution is asserted for this historical process. The status is unknown at the institutional level; the ending narrative explains its diffusion or development.
ending_narrative: The original renewal societies developed into distinct Methodist church structures while Wesleyan influence also continued outside them. There is no single date when Methodism as a movement dissolved. The American Methodist Episcopal Church is an important institutional development, not the sole replacement for all English Methodism.
